blocks.text: The chapter moves through three related scenes: Satan is bound while the faithful reign with Christ; Satan is released, gathers the nations, and is decisively defeated; then all the dead stand before the great white throne. The passage calls the martyrs’ life and reign the “first resurrection” and identifies the lake of fire as the “second death,” but these expressions have generated differing interpretations.

sections.title: The Millennium and the First Resurrection

blocks.text: The repeated “thousand years” organizes verses 1–10: Satan is bound for that period, the faithful reign with Christ during it, and Satan is released when it ends. Readers differ over whether this sequence should be understood primarily as chronological description or symbolic presentation. Likewise, the text names the martyrs’ life and reign the “first resurrection” without resolving every later doctrinal question about its nature or timing. Interpretation should therefore preserve what the vision clearly says without pretending that its disputed details are simple.

The chapter itself defines the “second death” as the lake of fire. Death and Hades are cast there, as are the devil, the beast, the false prophet, and anyone not found in the book of life. This distinguishes the second death from ordinary physical death: even Death and Hades surrender their dead for judgment before they themselves are removed.

The appearance of Gog and Magog belongs to Revelation’s repeated recomposition of imagery from Ezekiel. Revelation does not merely reproduce that earlier material; it places Gog, the gathered nations, the threatened holy community, and destruction from heaven within its own sequence of Satan’s final release and defeat.

The biblical hope of resurrection develops from scattered hints in the Old Testament into explicit New Testament proclamation. By the time of the earliest Christian message, resurrection had become central to its language of hope, judgment, and new creation. Revelation 20 participates in that larger development through its visions of the first resurrection and of all the dead appearing before the throne.

sections.title: Why Resurrection Was a Striking Claim

blocks.text: Resurrection hope stood out in cultures where death was commonly regarded as final. Bodily resurrection was also debated within Second Temple Judaism, so the New Testament proclamation was both rooted in an existing conversation and disruptive within it. This background clarifies why the sea, Death, and Hades giving up their dead is such a forceful picture: death cannot retain those summoned to judgment.

Across the book, Revelation repeatedly reworks imagery from Israel’s Scriptures, especially Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Exodus, Zechariah, Genesis, and Psalms. Its visions are therefore presented through a broad scriptural vocabulary rather than as isolated images.

sections.title: Death Does Not Have the Final Word

blocks.text: The resurrection setting helps explain the chapter’s significance: its judgment scene is not only about accountability but also about God’s power over death and the renewal of his people. The dead are not beyond his reach, and Death itself is finally judged. That relationship makes resurrection essential to the chapter’s movement from the reign of the faithful to the final removal of death.
